title: Space Force Awards Three Firms $615 Million for Satellite Target-Tracking Program
excerpt: Rocket Lab, STR, and a classified third company win contracts to develop space-based systems for detecting airborne threats, diversifying the Pentagon's satellite sensing capabilities.
body:
• The U.S. Space Force awarded $615 million in contracts to three companies — Rocket Lab, STR, and an unnamed third firm — to develop Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) satellites.
  • Rocket Lab received the largest share at $397 million and will develop next-generation "Flatellite" spacecraft launched on its Neutron rocket.
  • The awards follow a $4.6 billion contract to SpaceX in May, as the Pentagon diversifies its vendor base for the critical tracking mission.
  • The identity of the third company was withheld citing operational security concerns, reflecting a growing trend in Pentagon contracting.

The U.S. Space Force has awarded $615 million in contracts to three companies to develop satellites capable of detecting and tracking fast-moving airborne targets, marking a major push to diversify the Pentagon's space-based sensing capabilities beyond a single contractor.

Space Systems Command announced the awards to Rocket Lab, Massachusetts-based Systems & Technology Research (STR), and a third company whose identity was withheld for "operational security" reasons. The contracts represent the second round of task orders under the service's Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program.

Rocket Lab Lands Largest Share

Rocket Lab confirmed it received $397 million — the bulk of the total contract value. Under the deal, the company will develop, launch, and operate multiple advanced "Flatellites," a next-generation flat satellite design optimized for large constellations equipped with space-based sensors and low-latency, high-bandwidth communication links.

The satellites will launch aboard Rocket Lab's new Neutron heavy-lift rocket, which is expected to make its maiden flight between October and December from the company's launch complex on Wallops Island, Virginia.

"The core focus of this second task order is diversifying our capabilities and ensuring we don't rely on a single technical solution."

— Col. Ryan Frazier, Acting Space Based Sensing and Targeting Portfolio Acquisition Executive

Building Beyond SpaceX

The new contracts build on a massive $4.6 billion deal awarded to SpaceX in May to develop an initial satellite constellation for the SB-AMTI program. SpaceX also won a separate $1.6 billion contract to launch the future AMTI satellites. By bringing in three additional vendors, the Space Force aims to avoid dependence on a single technical solution.

"With these new partnerships, we are exploring unique innovations and technologies and fundamentally different ways to accomplish the airborne moving target indication mission," Frazier said. "Maturing these varied technical solutions now gives us distinct performance advantages for the future and guarantees we are fielding the absolute best technology available."

Why Space-Based Tracking Matters

The U.S. military has traditionally relied on ground-based radars and aircraft like the Air Force's E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets including missiles, aircraft, and drones. But those platforms have grown increasingly vulnerable to adversaries' anti-access and area-denial capabilities. Moving the mission to space promises greater survivability and eliminates operational blind spots that ground-based systems face.

The Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office are working together to add satellites to the target-tracking equation, an approach leaders expect will make the mission more resilient against sophisticated threats from China and other near-peer adversaries.

Classified Third Vendor Raises Questions

The Pentagon's decision to withhold the third company's identity reflects a broader trend. The military has increasingly cited operational security to protect developing capabilities from adversaries, declining to share details about contracts that were routinely disclosed in the past. This practice is enabled by non-traditional contract vehicles such as indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity agreements and Other Transaction Authorities that do not carry the public reporting requirements of standard Federal Acquisition Regulation contracts.

What's Next

The SB-AMTI program now represents over $6.8 billion in combined awards across multiple vendors, underscoring the Pentagon's commitment to building a robust space-based surveillance architecture. Rocket Lab's Neutron rocket debut later this year will be a key milestone, as the company races to prove its heavy-lift capabilities for national security missions. STR's contribution and the classified vendor's work will further define how the Space Force shapes its next-generation sensing architecture.
